advisory.title: Integer overflow in `BytesMut::reserve`
Invalid pointer dereference in `fmt::Pointer` impl for `Atomic` and `Shared` when the underlying pointer is invalid
advisory.description: Affected versions of `fmt::Display` dereference the underlying pointer. This causes a invalid pointer dereference e.g., when a pointer created with `Atomic::null` or `Shared::null`. `fmt::Debug` impls and pre-0.9 `fmt::Display` impls, which do not dereference pointers, are not affected by this issue.

advisory.title: h2 unbounded empty DATA frames
advisory.description:
The h2 crate, used internally by hyper, had a flaw that would accept and queue empty DATA frames without limit.
If streams were not actively drained, this could lead to unbounded memory usage, or a panic if the length overflows.

Low severity.

Patched in v0.4.16.

advisory.title: `libsqlite3-sys` via C SQLite CVE-2026-119375
advisory.description:
SQLite versions before 3.54.0 can return uninitialized page-cache memory when a process opens a database file together with a sibling write-ahead-log (`-wal`) file whose page size differs from the database's. A crafted pair of files can make ordinary queries return stale bytes from the process's memory. The attack vector is local and needs the victim to open the files.

As `libsqlite3-sys` bundles SQLite when it is built from its bundled source (the `bundled` feature, which `rusqlite`'s `bundled` feature enables), it is susceptible to the vulnerability. The releases `0.6.0` to `0.38.2` bundle SQLite `3.13.0` to `3.53.2` and are affected; the earlier releases contain no SQLite source. `libsqlite3-sys` was updated to bundle the patched version of SQLite in `0.39.0` (SQLite `3.54.0`) and `0.39.1` (SQLite `3.54.1`), released with [`rusqlite` 0.41](https://github.com/rusqlite/rusqlite/releases/tag/v0.41.0). `libsqlite3-sys` `0.39` declares Rust 1.88 and `rusqlite` `0.41` declares Rust 1.89.

Only a process that opens a database file, with its `-wal`, that a less trusted party could have written is exposed. A build that links a system SQLite instead of the bundled source is not affected by the copy in this crate; its exposure is that of the system library's version. The `bundled-sqlcipher` feature builds SQLCipher instead of SQLite; in `0.39.0` and `0.39.1` it depends on `sqlcipher-src =419.0.6`, which bundles SQLite `3.53.4` and is affected.

advisory.title: Quadratic run time when checking a start tag for duplicate attribute names
advisory.description:
`BytesStart::attributes()` returns an `Attributes` iterator which, by default
(`with_checks(true)`), rejects a start tag that repeats an attribute name. For
each attribute yielded, the iterator compared the new name against every name
seen so far in the same tag using a linear scan, so a start tag with `N`
distinct attribute names cost `O(N²)` byte comparisons. There was no bound on
`N` other than the size of the buffered start tag.

## Impact

Any code that parses untrusted XML and iterates a start tag's attributes with
the default duplicate check enabled can be made to spend CPU time quadratic in
the number of attributes on a single tag. Because the check is pure computation
with no `.await`/I/O, an I/O-based timeout on the consumer (for example a read
or request timeout) cannot interrupt it while it runs.

Measured cost of a single start tag, release build:

| Attributes on one tag | Time |
|---|---|
| 80,000  | ~6 s   |
| 800,000 | ~10 min |

The cost grows with the square of the attribute count, so a start tag of a few
tens of megabytes can stall a parsing thread for hours. No memory is exhausted
and the parser does not crash; the effect is CPU exhaustion on the thread doing
the parsing: a single crafted start tag can pin a CPU core for minutes to hours,
denying service to that worker. A deployment that places a wall-clock bound on
parsing, or confines it to a non-critical thread, may consider the availability
impact lower.

## Affected code paths

* `BytesStart::attributes()` / `Attributes` iterated with checks enabled (the
  default), and `BytesStart::try_get_attribute`.
* `NsReader`, which resolves namespaces by iterating a tag's attributes and so
  reaches the same check internally.

Consumers that iterate attributes with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` and do
not use `NsReader` are not affected.

This was reported as reachable by a remote, unauthenticated attacker in a
real-world RPKI relying party (NLnet Labs Routinator) via a crafted RRDP
`snapshot.xml`.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `quick-xml >= 0.41.0`, where the duplicate check keeps the linear
scan for start tags with a small number of attributes and switches to an `O(1)`
hash pre-filter above a threshold, making the whole tag `O(N)`. The reported
`AttrError::Duplicated` positions are unchanged.

If upgrading is not possible and duplicate-name detection is not required,
disable it with `.attributes().with_checks(false)` (this does not help
`NsReader` consumers, which have no equivalent opt-out before 0.41.0).

advisory.title: Unbounded namespace-declaration allocation in `NsReader` enables memory-exhaustion denial of service
advisory.description:
`NsReader` resolves namespaces by calling `NamespaceResolver::push` for every
`Start`/`Empty` event *before* the event is returned to the caller. `push`
iterated all `xmlns` / `xmlns:*` attributes on the start tag and, for each one,
appended the prefix bytes to an internal buffer and pushed a `NamespaceBinding`
(32 bytes on 64-bit) to an internal `Vec`, with no upper bound on the number of
declarations.

## Impact

A start tag with `N` namespace declarations drove roughly `3×` the tag's byte
size in `NamespaceResolver` heap, allocated *inside* `quick-xml` before the
`NsReader` consumer ever received the event and could inspect or reject it. A
consumer that bounds its *input* size therefore still cannot bound this
allocation: an `M`-byte start tag yields on the order of `3 × M` bytes of
resolver heap the caller never sees.

On untrusted XML this lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker force large heap
allocations with a single start tag. With several `NsReader`s running
concurrently on independent inputs (a common server pattern), the allocations
stack and can exhaust process memory, causing the operating system to kill the
process (OOM). This was confirmed against a real-world RPKI relying party (NLnet
Labs Routinator), where concurrent RRDP validation workers parsing a crafted
`snapshot.xml` exceeded the memory limit and the process was OOM-killed.

## Affected code paths

Consumers using `NsReader` (which always calls `NamespaceResolver::push` before
yielding `Start`/`Empty`), or calling `NamespaceResolver::push` directly. A plain
`Reader` that does not perform namespace resolution is not affected.

## Remediation

Upgrade to `quick-xml >= 0.41.0`. `NamespaceResolver::push` now rejects a start
tag that declares more than `DEFAULT_MAX_DECLARATIONS_PER_ELEMENT` (256)
namespace bindings, returning the new `NamespaceError::TooManyDeclarations`
instead of allocating without limit. The limit is configurable via
`NamespaceResolver::set_max_declarations_per_element` (use `usize::MAX` to
restore the previous unbounded behavior), and `NsReader::resolver_mut()` is
provided to reach it.

There is no clean workaround for `NsReader` consumers before 0.41.0, as the
allocation happens inside the reader with no configuration knob to cap it.

advisory.title: `Debug` impls for client session values expose TLS secrets
advisory.description:
The `Debug` implementations of `Tls12ClientSessionValue` and
`Tls13ClientSessionValue` were derived, and so included the TLS 1.2 master
secret or TLS 1.3 resumption PSK in their output.

Custom `ClientSessionStore` implementations that format these values with
`Debug` (for example, when logging) could disclose these secrets to readers of
the logs. This conflicts with rustls's
[key-material redaction policy](https://github.com/rustls/rustls/blob/99f2358cae2954837dbb866faf6727de75489ab9/SECURITY.md#boundary-public-api).

Ordinary connection and built-in session cache `Debug` output is redacted and
is not affected.

advisory.title: Unauthenticated ServerHello can downgrade later connections to classical key exchange
advisory.description:
The client recorded the server-selected key exchange group for each server
name when processing the ServerHello, before the server was authenticated.
This record is used to predict which key share to send in future ClientHellos
to that server name.

A network attacker can answer one connection attempt with a ServerHello
selecting X25519, and then close the connection. Later ClientHellos for that
name carry only an X25519 key share, while `supported_groups` still lists
X25519MLKEM768 first. If the genuine server accepts that share rather than
sending a HelloRetryRequest for its preferred hybrid group, the handshake
completes with classical-only key exchange and no error. This persists for as
long as the entry stays in the client's session store.

The impact is loss of post-quantum confidentiality for affected connections
("harvest now, decrypt later"). There is no key compromise and no
authentication bypass.

The following are not affected:

- connections to servers which send a HelloRetryRequest for their preferred group,
- clients with resumption disabled (as nothing is stored), and
- other server names.

This behaviour is discussed in
[draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-tls-key-share-prediction-01.html#name-security-considerations),
so the practical impact depends largely on server policy.

advisory.title: Brotli certificate decompression can allocate up to 1 GiB before authentication
advisory.description:
The built-in Brotli certificate decompressor (enabled by the non-default
`brotli` crate feature) bounded the size of the decompressed output, but
accepted a peer-selected history window. Brotli's large-window extension was
enabled, so a five-byte header could cause an allocation of 1 GiB. A peer can
abort a process whose allocator cannot satisfy that request.

No trusted certificate is required by the attacker. Affected configurations are:

- clients that enable the `brotli` feature and connect to a malicious server, and
- servers that enable the `brotli` feature and request client certificates.

Applications that do not enable the `brotli` feature are not affected.

advisory.title: TLS 1.3 handshake messages incorrectly accepted across encryption level boundaries
advisory.description:
Rustls accepted TLS 1.3 handshake messages sent at the wrong encryption level
when they followed a key-changing message in the same record. For example,
a plaintext `EncryptedExtensions` message packed into the same record as the
`ServerHello` was accepted.

RFC 8446 section 5.1 requires that handshake messages do not span key changes,
and that implementations terminate the connection with an "unexpected_message"
alert if they do.

The handshake transcript is still authenticated, so a network-position attacker
cannot use this to alter or complete a handshake; the practical effect is that
a peer could send handshake messages that should be encrypted in plaintext
without rustls rejecting the connection.

This is functionally the same bug as Go's
[GO-2026-4340](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-4340) (CVE-2025-61730).

advisory.title: CRLs not considered authoritative by Distribution Point due to faulty matching logic
advisory.description:
If a certificate had more than one `distributionPoint`, then only the first `distributionPoint` would be considered against each CRL's `IssuingDistributionPoint` `distributionPoint`, and then the certificate's subsequent `distributionPoint`s would be ignored.

The impact was that correctly provided CRLs would not be consulted to check revocation. With `UnknownStatusPolicy::Deny` (the default) this would lead to incorrect but safe `Error::UnknownRevocationStatus`. With `UnknownStatusPolicy::Allow` this would lead to inappropriate acceptance of revoked certificates.

This vulnerability is thought to be of limited impact. This is because both the certificate and CRL are signed -- an attacker would need to compromise a trusted issuing authority to trigger this bug.  An attacker with such capabilities could likely bypass revocation checking through other more impactful means (such as publishing a valid, empty CRL.)

More likely, this bug would be latent in normal use, and an attacker could leverage faulty revocation checking to continue using a revoked credential.

This vulnerability is identified as [GHSA-pwjx-qhcg-rvj4](https://github.com/rustls/webpki/security/advisories/GHSA-pwjx-qhcg-rvj4). Thank you to [@1seal](https://github.com/1seal) for the report.

advisory.title: Certificate verification may accept distrusted intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys when the configured trust anchors allow such paths.
The private keys corresponding to these intermediates are now well known.

Versions 0.103.16 and 0.104.0-alpha.8 reject paths containing these public keys.

advisory.title: Reachable panic in certificate revocation list parsing
advisory.description:
A panic was reachable when parsing certificate revocation lists via [`BorrowedCertRevocationList::from_der`]
or [`OwnedCertRevocationList::from_der`].  This was the result of mishandling a syntactically valid empty
`BIT STRING` appearing in the `onlySomeReasons` element of a `IssuingDistributionPoint` CRL extension.

This panic is reachable prior to a CRL's signature being verified.

Applications that do not use CRLs are not affected.

Thank you to [@tynus3](https://github.com/tynus3) for the report.

advisory.title: Name constraints were accepted for certificates asserting a wildcard name
advisory.description:
Permitted subtree name constraints for DNS names were accepted for certificates asserting a wildcard name.

This was incorrect because, given a name constraint of `accept.example.com`, `*.example.com` could feasibly allow a name of `reject.example.com` which is outside the constraint.
This is very similar to [CVE-2025-61727](https://go.dev/issue/76442).

Since name constraints are restrictions on otherwise properly-issued certificates, this bug is reachable only after signature verification and requires misissuance to exploit.

This vulnerability is identified as [GHSA-xgp8-3hg3-c2mh](https://github.com/rustls/webpki/security/advisories/GHSA-xgp8-3hg3-c2mh). Thank you to [@1seal](https://github.com/1seal) for the report.

advisory.title: Name constraints for URI names were incorrectly accepted
advisory.description:
Name constraints for URI names were ignored and therefore accepted.

Note this library does not provide an API for asserting URI names, and URI name constraints are otherwise not implemented.  URI name constraints are now rejected unconditionally.

Since name constraints are restrictions on otherwise properly-issued certificates, this bug is reachable only after signature verification and requires misissuance to exploit.

This vulnerability is identified as [GHSA-965h-392x-2mh5](https://github.com/rustls/webpki/security/advisories/GHSA-965h-392x-2mh5). Thank you to [@1seal](https://github.com/1seal) for the report.

advisory.title: Denial of Service via Stack Exhaustion
advisory.description:
## Impact

When user-provided input is provided to any type that parses with the RFC 2822 format, a denial of
service attack via stack exhaustion is possible. The attack relies on formally deprecated and
rarely-used features that are part of the RFC 2822 format used in a malicious manner. Ordinary,
non-malicious input will never encounter this scenario.

## Patches

A limit to the depth of recursion was added in v0.3.47. From this version, an error will be returned
rather than exhausting the stack.

## Workarounds

Limiting the length of user input is the simplest way to avoid stack exhaustion, as the amount of
the stack consumed would be at most a factor of the length of the input.

advisory.title: Bundled root certificates allow trust in distrusted emSign intermediates
advisory.description:
Affected versions include `emSign ECC Root CA - G3`, which can allow certificate
paths through distrusted emSign intermediates.

Affected versions may accept certificate paths containing distrusted emSign
intermediate public keys. The private keys corresponding to these intermediates
are now well known.

Version 1.0.10+ removes this root.

The `webpki-roots` 0.26.11 compatibility package contains no independent trust
store and re-exports the roots from its separately resolved 1.x dependency.
That parent dependency must resolve to 1.0.10 or newer; an older parent remains
affected by this advisory.

advisory.title: zip: `ZipArchive::extract` creates symbolic links whose attacker-controlled targets are outside the destination directory
advisory.description:
In `zip` 9.0.0-pre2, `ZipArchive::extract` creates a symbolic link from an archive entry after validating only the output entry path. The link target bytes are passed directly to the platform symlink API, so a malicious archive can create an entry inside the destination that resolves to an attacker-chosen path outside it. This behavior was verified on macOS and Linux. On either platform, a subsequent application read or write through that extracted entry accesses the external target with the extracting process's permissions.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-4v9h-p7m9-rh26

advisory.title: zip: `ZipArchive::extract` aborts the process on a symlink entry with a large declared size
advisory.description:
`ZipArchive::extract()` sizes the symlink-target buffer from the uncompressed
size declared in the central directory record, before reading a single byte of
entry data:

```rust
let mut target = Vec::with_capacity(file.size() as usize);
```

Both inputs are attacker-controlled. `ZipFile::size()` returns
`uncompressed_size` verbatim from the central directory, widened to a full `u64`
by a ZIP64 extended-information extra field, and is never cross-checked against
the compressed size, the remaining archive length, or any platform-appropriate
bound for a symlink target. `ZipFile::is_symlink()` is decided entirely by the
`S_IFLNK` bit of the external-attributes field.

`Vec::with_capacity()` is infallible: when the reservation is refused it calls
`handle_alloc_error()` and aborts the process. This is not a Rust panic. It is
not caught by `catch_unwind()`, is unaffected by `panic = "unwind"`, and is not
contained by running the call on a worker thread.

A 112-byte archive is sufficient. One `Stored` entry flagged `S_IFLNK` with a
ZIP64 field declaring `uncompressed_size = 2^62` and a zero-byte payload makes
`extract()` fail with:

```
memory allocation of 4611686018427387904 bytes failed
Aborted (core dumped)          # exit 134
```

The declared value only needs to exceed the host's address space, not its RAM:
`Vec::with_capacity()` maps address space without touching pages, so resident
memory stays flat and the abort happens on the refused reservation itself. Under
a `ulimit -v` cap or a memory-constrained container the threshold drops far
enough that a plain 32-bit `uncompressed_size` with no ZIP64 field suffices.

Applications that extract archives from untrusted input are affected on Unix and
Windows targets with default features and no special configuration: upload
handling, mail-attachment processing, package and artefact ingestion, backup
restore and container-image layer extraction. No confidentiality or integrity
property is affected: there is no memory unsafety, no out-of-bounds access, no
disclosure and no data corruption.

The fix landed in [zip-rs/zip2#984](https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/pull/984) and
shipped in 9.0.0.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-q7v9-x93c-xqv3

advisory.title: Insecure Preservation of SUID/SGID Bits during ZIP Extraction Leading to Potential Privilege Escalation
advisory.description:
The `zip` crate preserves privileged Unix permission bits (SUID, SGID, and sticky bits) from ZIP `external_attributes` during extraction, instead of masking them to safe permission bits. If a privileged process (for example, `root` in an installer, CI/CD pipeline, or container build) extracts an attacker-controlled ZIP archive using `ZipArchive::extract()` or the stream extraction API, files can be created as setuid-root or setgid. This behavior allows the creation of SUID/SGID files during extraction, which can lead to local privilege escalation depending on the execution environment.

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-vv5m-jxxh-4627

advisory.title: ZipStreamReader::extract() and ZipArchive::extract() apply Unix permissions through symlinks without confining the target
advisory.description:
`ZipStreamReader::extract()` applies Unix permissions through extracted symlinks without validating the symlink target stays within the destination

For further details see: https://github.com/zip-rs/zip2/security/advisories/GHSA-4684-h2q9-2vcp

advisory.title: Data from an abandoned stream leaks into the next stream on a reused context
advisory.description:
The `with_context` constructors of the stream encoders and decoders used the
borrowed context as it was. When a stream was abandoned on a context, for
example an encoder dropped before `finish()` after an error, whatever it
left there was carried into the next stream: the input buffered by the
previous encoder (up to 128 KiB, or all of it with `zstdmt`) became the
start of the next frame, and a decoder returned undelivered output of the
previous stream.

An application reusing one context for data that must stay separate, such
as different users' requests, could disclose one user's plaintext to
another. Whoever supplies the data can cause the abandonment with invalid
input.

The flaw was corrected by resetting the context's session in
`with_context`.

advisory.title: `Seekable::decompress` sets a `Vec` length beyond its capacity for offsets past the end
advisory.description:
`ZSTD_seekable_decompress` shortens the requested length to the end of the
data without checking that the offset is before it. For an offset past the
end, it returns a wrapped-around length without writing anything, and
`Seekable::decompress` passed that length to `Vec::set_len`.

With the `seekable` feature, whoever supplies the archive, or chooses the
offset, can leave the caller's `Vec<u8>` with a length far beyond its
capacity. Reading it then discloses neighbouring heap memory, and appending
to it corrupts memory. Offsets near `u64::MAX` can also hang the call.

The flaw was corrected by clamping requests to the end of the data, and by
checking every count reported by the C library against the buffer capacity.

advisory.title: Uninitialized memory exposed when streaming decompression of a legacy frame fails
advisory.description:
When decompression fails inside a legacy (zstd v0.4 to v0.7) frame, the
bundled zstd library reports the output buffer as fully written although
nothing was written. `DCtx::decompress_stream` committed that position even
on error, and for a `Vec<u8>` destination this extended the vector's length
over uninitialized memory.

Legacy support is enabled by default. A 5- or 6-byte corrupt legacy frame is
enough: through `zstd::stream::write::Decoder`, up to 32 KiB of stale heap
memory is then passed to the wrapped writer on the next `write()` or
`flush()`, or when an `auto_flush()`/`on_flush()` decoder is dropped. Whether
this reaches an attacker depends on where the application sends the
decompressed output. `zstd::stream::read::Decoder`, `zstd::decode_all` and
the bulk API are not affected.

Before zstd-safe 4.0.0, output buffers could only be initialized slices.
The zstd crate's own writer had the same flaw from 0.4.22 to 0.7.x, which is
covered by a separate advisory.

The flaw was corrected by only committing the buffer positions of a
successful call.

advisory.title: WebAssembly allocator shim corrupts memory on allocation failure
advisory.description:
On wasm32, zstd-sys provides `malloc` and `free` to the C library through a
shim over Rust's allocator. The shim did not check for allocation failure:
it wrote its size header to address 0 and returned address 4, which the C
library used as a valid buffer. `free(NULL)` also read below address 0.

Whenever the instance cannot grow its memory by what a frame asks for, a
small crafted frame (a 9-byte header declaring a 128 MiB window is enough)
made decompression write decoded data over the bottom of the module's
linear memory, instead of failing. The corruption stays within the wasm
sandbox.

The flaw was corrected by returning NULL on allocation failure or size
overflow, and by making `free(NULL)` a no-op.

advisory.title: fxhash - no longer maintained
advisory.description:
The fxhash crate is no longer maintained.

The repository is stale and owner is no longer active on GitHub.

Please take a look at [rustc-hash](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustc-hash) instead.
```

advisory.title: paste - no longer maintained
advisory.description:
The creator of the crate `paste` has stated in the [`README.md`](https://github.com/dtolnay/paste/blob/master/README.md) 
that this project is not longer maintained as well as archived the repository

## Possible Alternative(s)

- [`pastey`]: a fork of paste and is aimed to be a drop-in replacement with additional features for paste crate
- [`with_builtin_macros`]: crate providing a [superset of `paste`'s functionality including general `macro_rules!` eager expansions](https://docs.rs/with_builtin_macros/0.1.0/with_builtin_macros/macro.with_eager_expansions.html)  and `concat!`/`concat_idents!` macros

[`pastey`]: https://crates.io/crates/pastey
[`with_builtin_macros`]: https://crates.io/crates/with_builtin_macros

advisory.title: `pin-utils` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The [upstream repository] was archived on October 1, 2026, after the
release of version 0.1.1.

For local pinning, replace `pin_mut!` with [`core::pin::pin!`], available
since Rust 1.68. For pin projection, replace `unsafe_pinned!` and
`unsafe_unpinned!` with [`pin-project`] or [`pin-project-lite`].

[upstream repository]: https://github.com/rust-lang/pin-utils
[`core::pin::pin!`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/pin/macro.pin.html
[`pin-project`]: https://crates.io/crates/pin-project
[`pin-project-lite`]: https://crates.io/crates/pin-project-lite

advisory.title: proc-macro-error is unmaintained
advisory.description:
proc-macro-error's maintainer seems to be unreachable, with no commits for 2 years, no releases pushed for 4 years, and no activity on the GitLab repo or response to email.

proc-macro-error also depends on `syn 1.x`, which may be bringing duplicate dependencies into dependant build trees.

## Possible Alternative(s)

- [manyhow](https://crates.io/crates/manyhow)
- [proc-macro2-diagnostics](https://github.com/SergioBenitez/proc-macro2-diagnostics)

advisory.title: rustls-pemfile is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The rustls-pemfile crate is no longer maintained. The repository has been archived since August
2025, and users are encouraged to depend directly on the underlying PEM parsing code included
in rustls-pki-types since 1.9.0. The latest version of rustls-pemfile is in fact a thin wrapper
around the same code used in rustls-pki-types, so migrating should be straightforward.

The new API is represented by the [`PemObject`][PemObject] trait, which provides methods for
reading a single or multiple PEM objects from a file or byte slice.

[PemObject]: https://docs.rs/rustls-pki-types/latest/rustls_pki_types/pem/trait.PemObject.html

advisory.title: `unic-char-property` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
All Unicode crates that are part of https://github.com/open-i18n/rust-unic are unmaintained.

## Recommended alternatives

- [`icu_properties`](https://crates.io/crates/icu_properties)

All Unicode crates that are part of https://github.com/open-i18n/rust-unic are unmaintained.

advisory.title: `zbus_names` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The `zbus_names` crate is no longer maintained as a standalone crate.

It has been merged into [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) starting with version `6.0.0`, as its `names` module.

Users should migrate to [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus), with its default features disabled if they only need the D-Bus name types.

advisory.title: `zvariant` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The `zvariant` crate is no longer maintained as a standalone crate.

It has been merged into [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) starting with version `6.0.0`, as its `wire` module.

Users should migrate to [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus), with its default features disabled if they only need the D-Bus wire format. Users of the GVariant format should migrate to [`zgvariant`](https://crates.io/crates/zgvariant).

advisory.title: `zvariant_derive` is unmaintained
advisory.description:
The `zvariant_derive` crate is no longer maintained as a standalone crate.

Its derive macros are provided by [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus) starting with version `6.0.0`.

Users should migrate to [`zbus`](https://crates.io/crates/zbus), with its default features disabled if they only need the D-Bus wire format.

advisory.title: Unsoundness in `Error::downcast_mut()`
`event-listener` allows `!Send` tags to cross thread boundaries via `StackSlot`
advisory.description:
Affected versions of `event-listener` unconditionally implement `Send` and
`Sync` for `StackSlot<'_, T>`, the stack-allocated listener type created
by the `listener!` macro.

This allows a `!Send` tag type set via `Event::with_tag` to be moved to
another thread and accessed via `StackSlot::wait`, causing a data race in safe
code.

advisory.title: Unsoundness in `Iterator` and `DoubleEndedIterator` impls for `glib::VariantStrIter`
advisory.description:
The `VariantStrIter::impl_get` function (called internally by implementations of the `Iterator` and `DoubleEndedIterator` traits for this type) was unsound, resulting in undefined behaviour.

An immutable reference `&p` to a `*mut libc::c_char` pointer initialized to `NULL` was passed as an argument to a C function that that mutates the pointer behind `&p` in-place (i.e. as an out-argument), which was unsound. After changes in recent versions of the Rust compiler, these unsound writes through `&p` now seem to be completely disregarded when building the `glib` crate with optimizations.

This subsequently caused all calls of `VariantStrIter::impl_get` to violate the safety requirements of the `std::ffi::CStr::from_ptr` function - which requires its argument to be a valid pointer to a C-style string - resulting in crashes due to `NULL` pointer dereferences.

This was fixed by passing the out-argument pointer explitly as `&mut p` instead of `&p`.

This issue has been present since this code was initially added in `glib` v0.15.0. The mismatch in mutability was likely missed (and not raised as an error by the compiler) because the C function wrapped by `VariantStrIter::impl_get` is variadic (`glib_sys::g_variant_get_child`), and the pointer in question is one of the variadic arguments.

advisory.title: Rand is unsound with a custom logger using `rand::rng()`
advisory.description:
It has been reported (by [@lopopolo](https://github.com/lopopolo)) that the `rand` library is [unsound](https://rust-lang.github.io/unsafe-code-guidelines/glossary.html#soundness-of-code--of-a-library) (i.e. that safe code using the public API can cause Undefined Behaviour) when all the following conditions are met:

- The `log` and `thread_rng` features are enabled
- A [custom logger](https://docs.rs/log/latest/log/#implementing-a-logger) is defined
- The custom logger accesses `rand::rng()` (previously `rand::thread_rng()`) and calls any `TryRng` (previously `RngCore`) methods on `ThreadRng`
- The `ThreadRng` (attempts to) reseed while called from the custom logger (this happens every 64 kB of generated data)
- Trace-level logging is enabled or warn-level logging is enabled and the random source (the `getrandom` crate) is unable to provide a new seed

`TryRng` (previously `RngCore`) methods for `ThreadRng` use `unsafe` code to cast `*mut BlockRng<ReseedingCore>` to `&mut BlockRng<ReseedingCore>`. When all the above conditions are met this results in an aliased mutable reference, violating the Stacked Borrows rules. Miri is able to detect this violation in sample code. Since construction of [aliased mutable references is Undefined Behaviour](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/nomicon/references.html), the behaviour of optimized builds is hard to predict.

advisory.title: `Array::insert` violates exception safety if compare function panics, leading to potential Double-Free
advisory.description:
In affected versions of this crate, `Array::insert` is not exception safe. In the `UPSERT` path, `key` and `value`'s snapshot is written to `self.data_block`, and after the insertion is completed, `key` and `value` are `mem::forget` in order to prevent double free. However, during the insertion, `K::compare` is invoked, which is a user-provided method. If user deliberately call panic in this function, during unwinding, the destructors of `key`, `value`, and `self` will all be called (since the `mem::forget` has not been called yet), leading to Double Free. Similar issues happens in the `!UPSERT` path.

The soundness issue was fixed in version `3.8.4` by using `ManuallyDrop` instead of `mem::forget`, and separating fallible code from infallible code during a node split - insert = insert_try -> insert_unchecked.

advisory.title: `AsyncFd::new` and related constructors violate I/O safety
advisory.description:
`tokio::io::unix::AsyncFd` provides safe constructors (`new`, `with_interest`, `try_new`, and `try_with_interest`) that accept any `T: AsRawFd` rather than requiring proof of ownership or validity of the file descriptor. Because `RawFd` implements `AsRawFd`, safe code can construct an `AsyncFd` from an arbitrary or closed file descriptor, or close/replace the underlying file descriptor while the `AsyncFd` is still alive.

This violates I/O safety in two ways:

1. `AsyncFd<T>` implements `AsFd` for all `T: AsRawFd` by calling `BorrowedFd::borrow_raw(self.as_raw_fd())`, allowing safe code to obtain an arbitrary `BorrowedFd<'_>` without owning the file descriptor.
2. Tokio's I/O driver stores a pointer to an internal allocation in the `epoll`/`kqueue` user data for registered file descriptors. If the underlying file descriptor is duplicated and then closed while an `AsyncFd` is alive, and the OS reuses that file descriptor number for a another IO resource on the same runtime, dropping the first `AsyncFd` deregisters the reused file descriptor number and frees the first while the original file description remains registered in `epoll`, leading to a use-after-free when a readiness event fires.

Starting in Tokio 1.51.6, 1.53.3, and 1.54.0, `AsyncFd::new`, `AsyncFd::with_interest`, `AsyncFd::try_new`, and `AsyncFd::try_with_interest` are deprecated in favor of the `unsafe` constructors `AsyncFd::register` and `AsyncFd::register_with_interest`. Callers must ensure that the file descriptor remains valid, open, and unchanged for the lifetime of the `AsyncFd`.

advisory.title: Use-after-free when changing a multithreaded context with an unfinished frame
advisory.description:
When a multithreaded frame (`zstdmt` feature, `CParameter::NbWorkers`) is
left unfinished, its jobs may still be running on the worker threads: the C
library only waits for them when the next frame starts, or when the context
is freed. A session reset makes the context accept changes again in the
meantime, so:

- unloading the dictionary (`load_dictionary`, `ref_cdict`, `ref_prefix`,
  `disable_dictionary`, `init*`, or `reset` with parameters) freed the
  dictionary a worker was still compressing against;
- changing `NbWorkers` made the next frame resize the job table before
  waiting for the old jobs.

The flaw was corrected by refusing these calls while a multithreaded frame
is unfinished. The new `CCtx::wait_for_workers()` waits for the workers
first.

advisory.title: `Seekable` reads a NULL or out-of-bounds seek table
advisory.description:
`Seekable` did not record whether it was initialized. On a fresh `Seekable`,
or one whose `init_buff()` failed, `decompress`, `offset_to_frame_index` and
`frame_decompressed_size` made the C library read a NULL seek table. After a
failed re-initialization, `decompress` returned data from the refused buffer
using the previous seek table.

Separately, `frame_decompressed_size(num_frames())`, on `Seekable` and
`SeekTable`, read one entry past the end of the seek table.

The flaw was corrected by refusing to use a `Seekable` until an
initialization succeeded, and by checking the frame index.

advisory.title: Heap buffer overflow in `CCtx::try_clone` on a multithreaded context
advisory.description:
`CCtx::try_clone` (`experimental` feature, deprecated) copies tables sized
from the context's applied parameters. Starting a multithreaded frame
(`zstdmt` feature) replaces those parameters with the workers' without
resizing the context's own tables, so after an abandoned single-threaded
frame, the copy wrote up to 512 KiB past a heap allocation, or read past
one. This became reachable with the bundled zstd 1.5.6.

The flaw was corrected by refusing `try_clone` (and the unsafe
`compress_block`) once `NbWorkers` was set on the context.

advisory.title: Out-of-bounds read in `train_from_buffer` when sample sizes overflow
advisory.description:
`ZDICT_trainFromBuffer` is never told the length of the samples buffer, so
`train_from_buffer` checked that the sample sizes add up to it. With
overflow checks off, as in release builds, that sum wrapped around: sizes
totalling 2^64 plus the buffer length passed the check, and the trainer read
past the end of the buffer. `zstd::dict::from_continuous` relies on this
check from zstd 0.4.10; older versions of zstd had their own, covered by a
separate advisory.

This requires the sample sizes to come from an untrusted source. The flaw
was corrected by summing the sizes with overflow checks.

advisory.title: Use-after-free with `CParameter::StableInBuffer`
advisory.description:
With `CParameter::StableInBuffer(true)` (`experimental` feature), the C
library keeps a pointer to the input of one streaming call and reads from it
in later calls, including `flush_stream` and `end_stream`, which take no
input. An `InBuffer` only borrows its slice for one call, so safe code could
free it in between, and freed memory was compressed into the frame. The C
library behaves this way since zstd 1.5.4, whether bundled or linked from the
system.

The flaw was corrected by refusing to enable the parameter.

advisory.title: Double free in `DCtx::try_clone`
advisory.description:
`DCtx::try_clone` (`experimental` feature, deprecated) is a plain copy of the
C context. A context owning a dictionary (from `load_dictionary`,
`ref_prefix` or `init_using_dict`) or a dictionary table (`ref_ddict` with
`RefMultipleDDicts`) ended up with both copies freeing it. A context cloned
mid-frame resumed on uninitialized stream state. The clone also silently lost
the `WindowLogMax` limit.

The flaw was corrected by refusing to clone such contexts, and by carrying
over the parameters the copy leaves out.

advisory.title: Use-after-free of a dictionary after a one-shot call on a context with an open stream
advisory.description:
The one-shot `DCtx` and `CCtx` methods assumed the C library resets the
context, but it leaves an open stream as it is. When a stream was left
unfinished on a context, a one-shot call such as `decompress_using_dict`
could leave the context pointing at the dictionary borrowed for that call,
and the next streaming call resumed the stream against it after it was
freed: decompressed output then contained freed heap memory. On the
compression side, the stream resumed against the one-shot call's buffers.

This requires an application to use one context for both streaming and
one-shot calls without a reset in between. The flaw was corrected by
resetting the session after one-shot calls whenever a stream may be open.

advisory.title: `OutBuffer::around_pos` exposes uninitialized memory
advisory.description:
`OutBuffer::around_pos` accepted a position past the initialized length of a
`Vec<u8>`. The next streaming call then marked everything before the
position as initialized, so safe code could read stale heap memory between
the vector's previous length and that position.

The flaw was corrected by zero-filling that gap.

advisory.title: Use-after-free through `init_using_cdict` and `init_using_ddict`
advisory.description:
`CCtx::init_using_cdict` and `DCtx::init_using_ddict` (`experimental`
feature, deprecated) took the dictionary as `&CDict<'b>` and `&DDict<'b>`
with only `'b: 'a`, so the dictionary itself could be dropped while the
context still pointed at it. The same mistake in other constructors was
fixed earlier (<https://github.com/gyscos/zstd-rs/issues/365>).

The flaw was corrected by taking `&'a CDict<'b>` and `&'a DDict<'b>`.

advisory.title: Out-of-bounds read with an out-of-range `InBuffer::pos`
advisory.description:
`InBuffer`'s fields are public, so safe code can set `pos` past the end of
`src`. The position was passed to the C library unchecked, and
`ZSTD_seekable_compressStream`, unlike the other streaming functions, does
not validate it: it read past the end of the input slice, by up to the
frame size, and compressed that memory into the output.

The flaw was corrected by checking the position before every call into the
C library.
